name: 酒ト飯 みすず (Sake to Meshi Misuzu)

claims.text: Tempura and tatsuta-age (wheat-battered or wheat-starch fried chicken) are menu staples; no dedicated fryer information was found, so shared-fryer cross-contamination must be assumed.
No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce mentioned in any source; standard wheat-containing soy sauce is the baseline assumption for marinades, dipping sauces, and braised dishes.
Chawanmushi (egg custard) and dashi-based broth dishes are standard on the menu; fish-based dashi stock is the default in Japanese izakaya cooking and likely present across multiple dishes.
No allergy-handling policy or allergen menu was found in any source reviewed. Diners with dietary restrictions should call ahead (079-263-7936) or enquire in Japanese on arrival.
Reservations accepted by phone or online, giving diners the opportunity to ask about ingredients in advance.
小麦粉は一部メニューのみ使用、トーストも提供＝共用調理環境。要相談。
自家製麹調味料は有機だが、醤油・味噌の小麦・大麦有無は未確認。要確認。
有機卵・乳を使うメニューもあり、ヴィーガンは要指定。
『調理にはなるべく小麦粉や砂糖を使っていない』。バターナッツかぼちゃのハンバーグは小麦粉不使用で作れる。
有機・無添加・無農薬食材のみ使用、自家製麹調味料はグルテンフリー。多くの料理が小麦粉不使用。

name: 讃岐うどん めんめ (Sanuki Udon Menme)

claims.text: Wheat is the kitchen's only product — udon noodles are made from wheat flour on-site daily. Cross-contamination with wheat is unavoidable throughout the entire operation.
The signature menme udon uses dashi soy sauce (だし醤油), which is wheat-containing. No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere.
Bonito flakes (鰹節) are a primary topping on the signature dish and are present throughout the kitchen. Fish-based dashi is the foundation of the broth. No vegan-safe preparation path exists.

No allergy menu, allergen sheet, or staff allergy-handling procedure is documented on any source reviewed. Given the language environment (Japanese-only) and the simplicity of the operation, allergy communication would be very difficult.
Sarashina soba typically contains wheat flour mixed with buckwheat; wheat flour is also used for tempura batter in the same small kitchen, creating high cross-contamination risk.
Tsuyu (soba broth/dipping sauce) at traditional soba restaurants is made with standard wheat-based soy sauce (shoyu); no tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned.
Katsuo (bonito) dashi is the standard base for soba tsuyu at Sarashina-style shops; shrimp tempura is also on the menu, making animal-product contact unavoidable.
No allergy menu, allergen labeling, or accommodation policy is mentioned on any platform. Cash-only, no-reservation shop with no English materials; allergy communication would require Japanese.

Buckwheat (soba) itself is inherently gluten-free, and zaru soba (cold plain buckwheat without tsuyu) could reduce exposure — but staff communication barriers and shared kitchen make this unreliable for celiac diners.
Tempura (shrimp, conger eel) is a core menu item, meaning wheat flour is in active use in the kitchen; no dedicated fryer or separate prep area is mentioned.
The house condiment is an oyster-dashi soy sauce (東丸のカキだし醤油) — a wheat-containing soy sauce used at table and almost certainly in cooking. No tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is listed.
Fish stock (dashi) is the base of udon soups and oden broth; shirasu, anago, and ebi are prepared throughout the kitchen. No plant-only cooking area exists.

The restaurant notes halal accommodation is available upon special arrangement, suggesting some dietary flexibility, but no mention of gluten or allergen handling protocols appears on any public source.

Credit cards accepted (Visa, Mastercard, Amex, JCB, Diners), multilingual menus available, and barrier-free access including wheelchair and sign language services — logistics are well handled even if dietary accommodation is limited.

name: 四季と創和の酔い処 ひより (Shiki to Souwa no Yoidokoro Hiyori)

claims.text: Tempura is a core menu item (fresh fish and seasonal vegetable tempura appear in the standard course), meaning wheat flour is actively used in the kitchen. Cross-contamination for celiacs must be assumed.

No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned. Standard wheat-containing soy sauce (醤油) is standard in Japanese kappo cooking and almost certainly used across sashimi, grilled, and vinegared preparations.
Fish-based dashi (鰹・昆布) is foundational to Japanese kappo cuisine and will be present in soups, vinegared dishes, and sauces. No plant-based dashi alternative is noted anywhere.
No allergy handling policy is published. The restaurant is a small 17-seat counter operation; direct phone contact (080-3818-0270) before visiting is the only viable path for allergy inquiries.
The owner hand-selects ingredients daily at market, suggesting flexibility around what goes into each dish — a potential opening for custom requests if communicated in advance in Japanese.
Wheat noodles are cooked in shared broth and water; no separate preparation area for allergen-free orders exists in this small counter-only kitchen.
The broth is seasoned with standard Japanese soy sauce (醤油), which contains wheat as a primary fermentation ingredient. Salt ramen style does not mean wheat-free.
The entire menu is animal-based (chicken and pork stock, chashu pork, gyoza with meat filling). There is no plant-based preparation track.

No allergen menu, allergy handling protocol, or dietary accommodation has been documented at this shop. Cash-only counter service with no reservation system suggests limited ability to arrange special orders in advance.

No dedicated gluten-free kitchen confirmed. The shop prepares and sells wheat-containing items (taiyaki, obanyaki, fu manju) alongside naturally wheat-free items (kuzu mochi, warabi mochi). Cross-contamination risk cannot be ruled out.
Mitarashi dango is listed as a menu item; mitarashi glaze is made with soy sauce, which in Japan typically contains wheat. No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternative noted.
No information on whether dairy or egg is used in any products. Taiyaki batter traditionally contains egg and milk. No vegan-specific handling protocol found.

No allergen handling information, staff training documentation, or allergy communication protocols found across any reviewed source. Recommend calling ahead at 0120-11-3977 to ask about specific items.

Core items like kuzu mochi and warabi mochi are made from naturally gluten-free, plant-based starches (kuzu root, bracken fern) with sugar and water — inherently free of wheat, dairy, and eggs when made traditionally.
